subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE  CONTRADICTION OF STATEMENT MADE IN HOUSE
MR. HERRIDGE  CONTRADICTION OF STATEMENT MADE IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question which affects a fundamental privilege of this house and its members. This privilege is the absolute right of a member to make a statement in the house and not to have its truth impeached or questioned in any place outside the house.
I refer to Beauchesne, fourth edition, citation 117, which reads as follows:
(1)	The privilege of freedom of speech enjoyed by members of parliament is in truth the privilege of their constituents.
(2)	Freedom of speech is declared by the Bill of Rights in the following terms: "That the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of parliament."
On October 16, 1963, I asked the following question of the Prime Minister, as reported at page 3632 of Hansard:
I ask the Prime Minister whether, in the spirit of fair play, he can inform the house as to the nature of the business which the Minister of Agriculture and his alter ego, the expectant Minister without Portfolio, considered so much more important than the debate and the votes on agricultural policy that they found it necessary to be absent for such a considerable time during the debate yesterday.
The Prime Minister replied as follows:
The Minister of Agriculture and his associate, having taken part in this debate on agriculture, left the house to attend engagements previously undertaken for the Minister of Agriculture with farmers of Canada in the west. They got in touch with the grass roots while the hon. member remained in the house.
On Thursday, October 17, 1963 a newspaper, the Oakville daily Journal Record, impeached the answer of the Prime Minister in the following words:
The daily Journal Record learned late today that agriculture minister Harry Hays was working an auction in Kingston when absent from parliament on Tuesday.
Prices of up to $1,000 were realized at the cattle sale conducted by Hays Farms Limited, formerly owned by Hays and now operated by his brother, Tom, of Oakville.
Hays auctioned at the second annual sale for Eastern Breeders Incorporated. A total of $25,135 changed hands.
He has earned up to $50,000 a year from auctioneering.
On Friday, October 18, 1963 the same newspaper repeated its impeachment in an editorial entitled "Hays was at Auction-His Place was in Ottawa". The concluding paragraph of this editorial reads as follows:
Meantime, we suggest again, if Harry Hays is to continue as Minister of Agriculture he keep to government business and keep out of the bull ring. Where public duty and public confidence is concerned, there should be no compromise.
I accepted, and I continue to accept, the truth of the Prime Minister's statement to me as a statement of fact, that is until it is proven or confessed to be untrue.

The question of the order of seating is one that is dealt with in the report, and the other question that seems to have arisen, and perhaps deserves to have a word or two said about it, is the question of recognition of certain members as a group or a party. I confess I am not subtle enough to be able to tell the difference between a group and a party. In my view, since parliament does not know the words, since our law does not know either of the words, and since they have no official connotation in any way, it does not matter which one is used.
I remember the days when the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and most of those who now support him used to refer to their party as a movement and resented very much having it called a party. I always thought that was a kind of sanctimonious distinction without a difference, and I think the same is true of this question of groups and parties. I think if any four or five of us in the house are gathered together under one leader we can call ourselves a group or a party, and it is nobody else's business what we call ourselves in a free country, so long as we do not try to pass ourselves off as somebody else.
Now, sir, there are two possible ways in which this question could have been resolved, and the committee considered both of them. One was what I would call the historic, traditional and chronological method; that is to

say, to look at the groups that are in the house and see which one had been around the longest and which had representation in parliament the longest and give it a priority, and then the one that had been next longest, and so on.

A certain recognition is given to ministers, especially to the Prime Minister as the real leader of the house. Apart from that, recognition is given as a courtesy, and solely as a courtesy. I do not see how it could be anything else unless we were fundamentally to alter the character of our parliament, which is divided into two sides with a government and an opposition. However, this recognition by courtesy has been given since 1921, and I think it is far too late to change the practice now. It does seem to me, Your Honour, that whether you seek the advice of parliamentary counsel or not, this is a matter which you will decide yourself in your own good time.

Mr. Speaker, following the example set by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), I shall be very brief. However, I have a few comments to make on his motion.
In the first place I must say that I was a member of the committee on privileges and elections to which the matter was referred. As the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) knows quite well, I do not agree completely with his ideas, especially regarding monetary reform. I also entertain some doubts as to whether the group led by the hon. member for Villeneuve is actually a party in the traditional sense of the word.
I tried to set forth the difficulties which might crop up if the committee were to decide that the group headed by the hon. member for Villeneuve did constitute a political party.
As for me, I do not feel that the committee should be called upon to decide whether or not this is the case. However, this problem has been brought before the committee and the house. It must be recognized that the Ralliement des creditistes has actually broken

off from the national Social Credit party. That is the first point. It must be recognized from the evidence in the house, that the group headed by the hon. member for Villeneuve is the larger one and that, on the other hand, having well established structures it has a right to be heard as a group. In addition, it seems to me that it is entitled to the privileges usually granted to a group.
That group is, after all, a physical entity, and must be assigned a specific seating space in the house. When the famous French poet Lamartine was elected deputy, he proclaimed he would like to be seated right under the ceiling. Unfortunately, that would not do in this house. That political group has a right to a material space in the house; it must be given a place.
That being said, it would seem to me that the only applicable criterion, which is both logical and consistent, is the numerical one. The hon. member for Villeneuve, and several other hon. members, have rightly pointed out that 13 is a larger number than 11. I feel there is no other principle which could guide the house in arriving at a fair and logical solution.
The Secretary of State has brought forth the argument of historical precedent. Even from this point of view I think that he is inconsistent in his argument. Indeed the principle of historical precedents has been abandoned for a number of years and is only taken up when there is a question of seating a group in the house, to determine its importance numerically. Moreover, if there is a question of seniority it should be kept in mind that the hon. member for Villeneuve, for whom I certainly hold no brief, was nevertheless, a member of this house from 1946 to 1949, and, as a matter of fact, for the riding of Pontiac which I am now representing. It is therefore clear that, in the Social Credit group, the hon. member for Villeneuve enjoys seniority.
For all those reasons I think that the house should not accept to concur in the report presented by the committee on privileges and elections, but that the house should rather refer the matter again to the committee for a new recommendation.
Moreover, it seems to me that the Secretary of State, who used to speak for freedom of speech, resorted to tactics which strangely resembled closure when, at about 4.20 last Friday, he moved the adjournment.
I hope that today he will not resort again to dilatory methods contrary to standing orders and to parliamentary tradition.
As the government, through his spokesmen the Secretary of State, as well as the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of

Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Turner), very clearly stated its stand in the matter, it should now assume its responsibilities without passing them on to others, and put an end to this controversy, once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. It is one which I think is of the utmost importance, namely that the House of Commons should not be made into a complete farce. At this moment we are, according to the precedence of orders, discussing a motion having to do with the seating and recognition of members in the House of Commons. In view of the fact that the economy of Canada might be brought to a standstill at any time, and that we are facing a most important issue affecting the entire country arising out of the trusteeship legislation and the shipping of Canada being brought to a halt, I would ask that we do not make a farce of the parliament of Canada at this time by discussing seating or the recognition of groups in the House of Commons.
I ask the Prime Minister or the house leader whether the necessary motion cannot now be moved so the House of Commons can discuss immediately the question of the trusteeship legislation, our shipping and what has taken place. Surely the economy of Canada is of more importance than the seating of members in this house or the recognition of groups. I ask the Prime Minister to take the necessary action now.

Mr. Speaker, when the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) says that there is no difference between a party and a group, I would answer him that there is, and a quite considerable one. In the report of the standing committee on privileges and elections, he states, in volume 3, that the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) should be seated on the left of the Social Credit party. Therefore, the group of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) is recognized as a party. The New

Democratic party, is recognized-the word party is mentioned-but when it comes to us, we are registered as a mere group.
Now, if the Secretary of State states that in this case there is no difference either, I want to state that when the motion is put and carried, they will find that there is a difference. But before we are accused of delaying the business of the house we certainly shall express our views and warn the government that it is taking a dangerous course and that, before long, it might come to regret its action.
Mr. Speaker, as I am interested in the motion now before the house, I think it is my duty to expound what I think might enlighten hon. members.
I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that when I was elected on April 8 last, for the second time, the electors of my county recognized that I was, first of all, a member of the Social Credit-and I still am-but the candidate chosen by the Ralliement des creditistes, and it was in that capacity that those electors financed my campaign.
Later on, you were informed at the Granby convention that we were not satisfied with our parliamentary leader and that we had decided to change him. At that time we agreed to choose a new parliamentary leader. Our present leader, our parliamentary leader, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) was chosen at a caucus. We saw in him qualities of dynamism and courage, and we wanted our whole country to benefit from that vitality.
The greater part of hon. members recognized that the division was justified. That is why I am asking the house to recognize our group according to our number. I shall come back to this matter in a while, in order fully to explain to hon. members that when we take tradition as a basis, the number is to be considered first.
If the question is of no interest to the members of other parties, they should let the group
I	represent in the house decide, and when the question is put we shall see where the true majority is and also which is the true Social Credit party.
If the house has decided that 12 members having a leader constitute a party, I wonder why it should delay the recognition of our group which comprises 13 members. Under Bill C-91, any group of at least 12 members will be officially recognized as a party in the house. As we have 13 members, we are therefore a party. The group of only
II	members cannot be called a party under Bill C-91.
To find the true definition of a party, one can consult the Quillet dictionary which says:
Privileges and Elections -of the union of several persons having the same interests or holding the same views against others who have opposite interests or views.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, we have in this house some interests with which all other parties disagree. Once again, this proves that we really form a party, and consequently, the definition of the Quillet dictionary applies.
We recognize also that the hon. member for Villeneuve has great merit. He gained the confidence of the people when, single handed, he had 26 members elected in 1962 and 20 in 1963. Without the fighting spirit of our leader, whose great qualities we recognize and which nobody can deny, I am convinced that the eleven members of the western group would not have been elected. Despite the stubborn fight conducted against the hon. member for Villeneuve, he succeeded in having 20 members elected last April, as you all know, and got 29 per cent of the votes, which is the second highest percentage in the province of Quebec. This is significant.
If this result scares the party in office and causes it to hesitate to recognize us as a fourth group in the opposition, it means that they will have to face our group after the next election, because the Ralliement des creditistes is the most dynamic group, and that, they know well. I therefore ask the government to reconsider their decision before they plunge into this, because it will have implications all across the nation.
I think that the New Democratic party, with 17 members, must sit right next to the official opposition party in this house. As far as we are concerned, we should sit on the left of the N.D.P. and as for the others they should sit in the corner, which seems logical since there are only 11 of them.
If one considers the votes taken lately, Mr. Speaker, one wonders whether there will be 11 of them very long, because they are divided into one, two or three groups, for 11 members. So, I wonder whether that pact will hold very long.
Since the reconvening of the session, you can see that we always stand united and that we know where we are going.
If there were an election tomorrow morning, if the people gave a solid vote for a new party, whatever its membership, could you, in two months from now, together with the new parties, count enough members to make up 140?
Do not forget that, because you are only a small group in the house. So, ask yourselves whether what you are doing is proper. But no, you do not ask yourselves that question. But the people want a new party, they want the party in power to hold a majority, and that is precisely decided by the number of members.

Privileges and Elections
If, after the last general election, the Liberals had been unable to assume office, they would have said: "Listen, we have 129 members whereas the Conservatives have only 94. It is unfair." As far as I am concerned, their complaints would have been justified because it is always the largest group which should have precedence.
In my opinion, you may live to regret this. I feel that we should do the same thing now that we did after the election of last April 8. It is only logical that the largest party should govern. However, it is obvious, here, that makeshift arrangements are being made.
Last year, with 30 members, we came before the New Democratic party which had only 17 members. We had precedence over them and we found that logical.
This year, the contrary is being done in the house, and I feel that such action is unfair to us.
In my opinion, the house should consider the question more seriously instead of contradicting itself as it has done in the past few days. Its actions contradict its statement.
I hope that the public which follows what is happening in parliament will not be deceived by the decision which the government has undertaken to have approved without further explanation. We know what the result would be, the same as last week.
The house wants to know if the Ralliement des creditistes constitutes a new party in this house. Well, we are not a new party, we still follow the Social Credit doctrine; we have only changed our leader in parliament. I claim that the majority voice is that of the largest number of members in a democratic party like ours or in a house where freedom of speech and freedom of action are recognized. Speaking of freedom of speech, if we are placed in fourth position, we will make our presence felt here, we will speak out and we will criticize you for this action every time we have the opportunity to do so.
You want to make us your scapegoats and give us the last place in the opposition. Do not forget that besides being a political group, we are a true political party as it is clearly recognized in the report of the privileges and elections committee.
If the word "party" is applied to the Social Credit party headed by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), or the New Democratic party, or to the Conservatives or the Liberals, I maintain that we are here as representatives of the Ralliement des creditistes and, therefore, constitute an officially recognized party. The dictionary proves us right as well as Bill C-91 for that matter. We are only asking you to be fair, and not only


in our own interests; indeed, we do not want a precedent to be thus created which we may have cause to regret later on. Some are here for this session only, but the younger ones among us, who can hope to spend many years in this chamber, do not want to deplore later an act that parliament is ready to approve today.
Another illogical situation is the alleged seniority of the group directed by the hon. member for Red Deer, the oldest group, the group which, it is said, professes the true Social Credit theory, whereas it is known that the hon. member for Villeneuve sat in the house from 1946 to 1949. It is therefore the hon. member for Villeneuve who would deserve that seniority and not the three other Social Credit members who belong to the group you wish to recognize and who were elected for the first time in 1957.
Consequently, I do not understand that position. They talk of seniority and then, looking at the senior members, they find there are three in one group and one in the other; now, as one group has three, that one is the real group.
Where is the seriousness, where is the logic of that reasoning? If we really desire to be fair and to be recognized as such throughout the country, I suggest to the house it is solely the number of members which should be the first consideration. As we are 13, we say that the true Social Credit group is the group of 13, and that until the next election.
That the group still bears the name of Social Credit, we agree and we are not ready to deny it; we shall keep the name. It is understood that we do not form a new group, we only have a new house leader; it is the same theory, and the proof is that ever since we came here, we have been sharing the same ideas as the other group, even though you do not want to admit our monetary theory.
I believe that if the party in office were to make a decision today, in view of the state of mind now prevailing, it would be shameful to see it proceed towards a precipice. As you have already done twice, at the time of your decisions on the 11 per cent tax and the legislation concerning old age pensions, this time again, you are running towards catastrophe.
I wish the people had trust in parliament for its passing proper legislation.
I wish I had heard not only the parliamentary secretary, who was far from being convincing that time, but also the Prime Minister, to see what he thinks about the situation.
The other day, I noticed he did not commit himself first, on the occasion of the vote, and I congratulate him. The hon. member for

Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) had said the first one to vote would take a great responsibility. It is therefore another one who assumed that responsibility.
Up to now we have heard backbenchers who did not really take this matter seriously. They sought to divert the attention of the house from the real problem and from the decision to be made. But we simply want our rights. No one can deny that we are not within our rights in trying to get what we are asking for.
We do not want to interfere with the business of the house and we would rather legislate and work for the people, but it is the respect for our rights that we are dealing with at this time. We sit now in the house and should a precedent be established, others in the years ahead would be placed in an unfortunate situation. We want the matter to be settled at once, even if it takes three or four days, we want it settled definitely so that we may arrive at a fair decision.
If tomorrow morning the leader of a party were to pass away, he would have to be replaced by another one, and the party would not lose its identity but the party leader would simply change. That is exactly what makes the difference.
In my opinion, the committee on privileges and elections spent too much time looking for considerations outside parliament. What has the national association got to do with that? It is members elected to the house who must reach their decisions. I think it is the word of the elected members which must count in the house and not considerations from outside.
At this time, it is useless to rack one's brains and look for difficulties where there are none in order to determine where is the real group. The national association has nothing to do with that. In my opinion, we have wasted enough time considering in this problem side issues which should have been disregarded altogether.
I should like to mention to the house all the admiration I have for my parliamentary leader, the hon. member for Villeneuve who offered last Friday the amount of his additional allowance of $4,000 to the down-and-out people in Canada. That proves again to the house that there has been no quibbling over that $4,000, but rather over the principle we wish to defend and that we do not want to see violated by others.
And when it is realized that, owing to internal difficulties in a group, it is virtually impossible to attain a preset goal, then one simply quits. But we did not, we took a vote and the majority decided that the ideal which it.
Privileges and Elections our group was pursuing was actually the one which we must reach.
I intend to move an amendment in the hope that it will be taken into consideration and that it will not be brushed aside too lightly. Things must not be rushed. It is much better to spend one or two extra hours today and reach a decision which parliament will not have cause to regret.
Everybody talks about democracy and about freedom. I would rather have spoken last Friday, as I could have waxed more eloquent after hearing various speeches on the same topic. But the Secretary of State prevented me from doing so at the time.
That is why I come back to this matter today, is to make hon. members realize our position, because I find that after two days outside parliament, opinions have not changed.
I simply ask the hon. members on the government side, before they vote, to think twice about the lack of fairness and of understanding they would show with regard to a group in this house, if they were to take a decision too quickly.
We simply ask to be recognized as a group of 13 in this house, and we want a place as such.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the report of the committee on privileges and elections be sent back to that committee with the recommendation from the house that the following words be added to paragraph 2:
"The house recognizes that the most elementary decency demands that it should not be up to other political parties to decide which of the two Social Credit groups is the Social Credit party, and proposes to leave it to the Social Credit members themselves to decide that point by a majority vote among the 23 Social Credit members."
Mr. Speaker, if the house would entertain that amendment, it could be said that it had acted in a truly democratic way, and one would see where democracy is to be found and what sensible results really are.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF APPOINTMENT OF NEW COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to announce that
the government has with regret accepted the resignation of Commissioner C. W. Harvison of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to take effect on October 31, 1963. Commissioner Harvison first submitted his resignation in April of this year at the termination of 35 years of service. At the request of the government he agreed to retain his post as commissioner for a further period but has now requested to be allowed to retire as of the end of October.
Commissioner Harvison joined the Royal North-West Mounted Police in 1919 and is the last serving officer who began his service in the force when it bore that historic name. Both in the ranks and as a commissioned officer he has not only participated in but has made a distinguished contribution to the development of the R.C.M.P. from a frontier police force into one of the finest modern law enforcement agencies of any country in the world.
On behalf of all members of the house and of the people of Canada may I express our sincere appreciation of Commissioner Harvi-son's long years of outstanding service to the country and to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He has good reason to be proud of his record, just as we can all take pride in the force he has served.
I should also like to announce that the governor in council has appointed Deputy Commissioner G. B. McClellan to succeed Commissioner Harvison, with effect from November 1,	1963. Deputy Commissioner
McClellan was born in Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, in 1908, was educated at the Royal Military College at Kingston, Ontario, and joined the R.C.M.P. in 1932. Commissioned in 1939, Deputy Commissioner McClellan has served in all fields of federal law enforcement and national security and has held increasingly responsible positions in which he contributed much to the growth and development of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Appointed deputy commissioner in 1959, he was responsible for the administration of the force until 1960 when he became deputy commissioner, operations, responsible to the commissioner for all phases of policing, security and investigational work of the force as the senior deputy commissioner, and second in command.
I am certain that Deputy Commissioner McClellan will carry out the heavy responsibilities of his new post in a manner in keeping with the fine traditions of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PORTUGAL-STATEMENT ON EXPORT OF ARMS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement about the policy of the government on the export of arms to South Africa, which the Prime Minister observed on Friday, October 11, was under consideration at that time by the government. 1 will also deal with the policy with regard to the export of arms to Portugal.
It has for several years been the policy of the Canadian government not to permit the shipment of arms to South Africa which might be used against the non-white population for the enforcement of the policy of apartheid. On August 7, 1963, the security council passed a resolution recommending that all states should cease the sale and shipment of arms, ammunition and military vehicles to South Africa. Taking into account the security council's recommendation and wishing further to express our disapproval of South Africa's apartheid policies, the government has decided that it will not authorize the acceptance of any new orders from South Africa for items of military equipment, nor permit the shipment of such equipment to South Africa.
Before August 7, 1963, the Canadian government had authorized the sale to South Africa of certain aircraft, communications equipment and air navigation equipment manufactured in Canada which were judged to be without relevance to the enforcement of the policy of apartheid. While keeping the situation under constant review, for the present the government will allow the shipment to South Africa only of maintenance spares for equipment supplied before August 7, 1963 and, subject to examination in each case, of certain aircraft piston engines and maintenance spares for such engines.
The government has also reviewed its policy with regard to the export of arms to Portugal. As I informed the house on June 25 this year, Canada has not made any contributions of Canadian military assistance to Portugal since November, 1960. With respect to the sale of arms and military equipment on a commercial basis, it has been the policy of the Canadian government since 1960 not to permit the export to Portugal or the territories under Portuguese administration of any arms or equipment which, in our judgment, would be used for military purposes in the Portuguese overseas territories. The government proposes to continue this policy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PORTUGAL-STATEMENT ON EXPORT OF ARMS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement made
[Mr. Pearson.l
by the minister is one of interest. It deals with a very difficult and trying problem. In its announcement the government has followed the course followed by the government of which I had the honour to be prime minister. I recognize the difficulties in the way.
So far as South Africa is concerned, we took the stand, and were greatly criticized for having done so, that while nations may practice in their hearts the luxury of discrimination, no nation within the commonwealth could have as its cornerstone a policy of discrimination as its only policy in dealing with those of a coloured race. As long as such a course was followed I contended, and the last year and a half has certainly borne out the stand I took, that within the commonwealth, with five out of six belonging to a coloured race, no nation could possibly accept membership believing, as does the present administration in South Africa, that a person belonging to a coloured race is not entitled to equality within the country.
In so far as Portugal is concerned, Portugal is the oldest ally of Great Britain. She has been a true ally throughout the years, as South Africa had been a true and co-operative friend in the commonwealth. It is difficult for a government to take a stand on this question and make the determination that has again been made. I think it is the only one consistent with the situation prevailing in the world today. I can only say that, difficult as the problem is, the government of the day having followed the path of the government of yesterday, which was criticized, we give our support to the stand taken.

I do not
want to belabour the point, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to express the suggestion that we lend our whole-hearted support to the statement the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just given to us. As one who perhaps understands well the situation because of years of experience in the continent about which we are talking, I am convinced that it is the responsibility of freedom loving people of Canada, with a parliamentary system of government, pledged to the preservation of the rights of individuals, regardless of race, colour or creed to give leadership whenever possible on problems such as this. I think the government has taken the correct stand in following the policies laid down by the previous government in regard to this most difficult problem.

subtopic: PORTUGAL-STATEMENT ON EXPORT OF ARMS FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about ten days ago I asked the Prime Minister what action the government intended to take with reference to stopping the shipment of arms to South Africa. I am very glad that the statement has been made

Questions
today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I think the government is to be congratulated for this somewhat belated decision to stop the shipment of arms to both South Africa and Portugal. I do not believe that under world conditions as they are today, Canada or the Canadian people would want arms shipped to South Africa which might be used to enforce apartheid and to carry on policies of racial discrimination. Nor do I think the Canadian people will support armaments being sent to Portugal in order to maintain the last relics of colonialism in that part of Africa.
I am very glad the government has taken the step which it has. I hope it will carefully watch the matter of aircraft because I am not sure I can agree with the minister when he says aircraft cannot be used to maintain apartheid policies. If there is civil disobedience in South Africa, certainly military aircraft would become very important weapons. I hope the government will watch carefully the question of airplanes and airplane parts going to South Africa. I am sure the statement which has been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs will be welcomed by Canadians generally as proof that we are doing more than paying lip service in our opposition to colonialism and racial discrimination.

It is a move forward in the recognition of human rights in a part of the world in which recognition is needed and help is needed. UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS TO CANADIANS WORKING IN MAINE
speechtext:
1.	On what date were the latest Canadian-Ameri-can interviews held or correspondence exchanged pertaining to the subject of Canadian forestry employees working in the state of Maine and unable to draw unemployment insurance?
2.	Who were the participating parties?
3.	On that occasion was any progress made?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS TO CANADIANS WORKING IN MAINE
speechtext:
1, 2 and 3. In view of the intense interest held by members from the areas of eastern Quebec and New Brunswick, it is felt that a complete statement should be made concerning the efforts to conclude a reciprocal agreement between the state of Maine and the unemployment insurance commission of Canada with respect to unemployment insurance.
The steps taken over the past year may be summarized as follows:
Discussions were held in Quebec city on 22 May, 1962, between the members of the Maine employment security commission, representatives of the U.S. bureau of employment security, representatives of importers for the American pulpwood association, and the members of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada.
While satisfactory progress appeared to have been made at this meeting, it was agreed at its conclusion that the members of the two commissions-Maine and the unemployment insurance commission-should meet again in October 1962.
On 22 and 23 August, 1962, the director of unemployment insurance and the chief of claims operations, both of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada, met with their counterparts from Maine to discuss administrative problems associated with any agreement that might be reached. These discussions were entirely satisfactory.

Questions
On October 19, 1962, the chairman of the Maine employment security commission wrote the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada stating that the question of a reciprocal agreement had been referred by the Maine commission to their advisory council and asking for a postponement of the proposed October meeting. The chairman of the unemployment insurance commission agreed.
In mid-December 1962, the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada telephoned his Maine counterpart regarding the postponed meeting and in reply received a letter dated December 17, 1962, from the Maine chairman to the effect that the advisory council would not be considering the matter of this agreement until its meeting on January 15, 1963, after which he would be pleased to arrange the meeting between the two commissions.
On January 17, 1963, the chairman of the Maine employment security commission again wrote the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada saying that the Maine advisory council had referred the question of this agreement to a special committee; that he would keep the unemployment insurance commission of Canada posted on further reports, and that he hoped for a meeting of the two commissions in the not too distant future to continue discussions.
On March 1, 1963, the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission of Canada enquired of the Maine commission as to the action taken by the advisory council and was informed that it (the council) was still gathering data pertinent to its deliberations.
On July 24, 1963, the chairman of the Maine employment security commission informed the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission that their commission had met with the advisory council and were now in process of making arrangements for a further discussion on the matter before a final decision is made. He further advised that he had hopes that the answer would be given to the unemployment insurance commission by September 1, 1963.
On August 1, 1963, the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission acknowledged the letter from the chairman of the Maine employment security commission expressing the hope that it will be possible to come to an agreement.
On August 20, 1963, the chairman of the Mains employment security commission wrote to the chairman of the unemployment insurance commission to report that due to unexpected difficulty in scheduling the meeting with the pulp and paper committee it ap-

peared that the earliest date for the meeting would be the middle of September and that a decision on the state of Maine-Canada reciprocal agreement would be communicated not later than October 1, 1963.
On September 25, 1963 discussions were held in Augusta, Maine regarding an agreement between the state of Maine and the unemployment insurance commission of Canada with respect to unemployment insurance. At the same time a meeting was held with the members of the employment security commission for the state of Maine. It is hoped that as a result of these further discussions a satisfactory conclusion can be reached.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CONFLICTING STATEMENTS RESPECTING PLANTING OF WHEAT
speechtext:
May I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce? In the address which
Inquiries of the Ministry the hon. gentleman delivered to the Saskatchewan farmers union on September 23 as reported in the Union Farmer he made an observation that it would be in the interest of western producers to devote less of their land to wheat than in the recent past. I should like to ask the minister if he can reconcile this advice with the statement made in Edmonton by the Minister of Agriculture on October 17, that there was an unlimited market for wheat grown by the Canadian farmer. I think the farmers would appreciate some direction as to what constitutes government policy; is it as enunciated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or by the Minister of Agriculture?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: CONFLICTING STATEMENTS RESPECTING PLANTING OF WHEAT
speechtext:
When I spoke on the subject I discussed the question of whether it would be necessary, looking ahead for some time-I was not talking about the need today, as the hon. member will see from reading the text of my remarks-to devote 27 million acres to wheat, which was the amount seeded this year, in order to supply the demand. I said in the course of my remarks that looking ahead for some years-and I did in fact project as far as 1980-one could see a large and growing demand for feed grains. In these circumstances it did seem to me that farmers, in planning for the future, might consider whether they would get more out of their land by continuing to devote as much to wheat as they did, or whether they should not consider diverting some to feed grains. That is the position I took and it is, I find, exactly the same position as was taken by the Manitoba minister of agriculture, Mr. Hutton, when he spoke in Winnipeg at the beginning of this month. He set out the same considerations.
These are the considerations one ought to bear in mind in the future, but, of course, before any advice is given to parliament the government will be considering the whole question in the light of the information which is available as we approach seeding time. I have been in Europe, and the impression I got was that the demand for wheat will continue at a fairly high level during the coming crop year. I hope that is right. If this should prove to be the case, information of this kind will be given to the farmers and to the farm organizations who will be able to make their decisions as to what to seed in the light of all the conditions and in the light of the best information we are able to place before them at the time.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege is raised now because this seems to be an opportune point at which to do it. I have put several questions on the order paper, as Your Honour will probably have noticed, and have received answers to about half of them. As I understand it, the placing of questions on the order paper is for two purposes; one is to save the time of the house in asking them as verbal questions on orders of the day, and the other is to obtain information that is public information and not classified as privileged.
The answers to questions so far from the government have been very sketchy indeed.


As one example I might quote to Your Honour the answer to my question 1,272 today. The second part of that question was:
Have the plans and specifications of the project been completed and, if so, when is it intended to call for public tenders on the job?
The answer to that is "No". This is typical of a good many of the answers that have been given. Together with the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac (Mr. Webb) I would ask, what is the point of asking questions unless there is going to be some effort made on the part of ministers of the crown to give more complete answers?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I should be permitted to say a word on the point of order, or question of privilege, whichever it is the hon. gentleman has raised.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Privilege.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I would draw attention to the fact that the order paper shows, as anyone can see, that well over 1,100 questions have already been answered in this parliament, which must be something of a record. I might say also that the hon. gentleman's example of a question was an exceptionally poor one, because he was not asking about something that had been done, but about something that might or might not be done in the future. It seems to me there is a rule of the house that hypothetical questions should not be asked or answered.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
On the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, the first part of that question was:
Does the government intend to proceed with the construction of a minimum security penal institution in the Yukon territory and, if so, where is the intended location of such institution?
The answer given to that part was complete and I am satisfied with it. But the second part of the question was:
Have the plans and specifications of the project been completed and, if so, when is it intended to call for public tenders on the job?
The answer given was "No". The answer to the third part of the question was:
It is anticipated that construction will begin in 1964, for completion in 1965.
This is an example of the incomplete answers we are getting. The Secretary of State is certainly no expert in the construction of questions. He knows, as any minister of the crown knows, what the questions mean. My questions are carefully thought out. I could ask them on the orders of the day and waste a good deal of the time of the house, just as the Secretary of State

used to do during the last session; but I am trying to co-operate, as is the hon. member for Hastings-Frontenac. Yet all we get is evasion and equivocation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
It would, I think, be too much to expect that I should not have a word to say in reply. The hon. member said he could waste the time of the house by asking questions. Surely if his questions are a waste of the time of the house they should not be asked on orders of the day, and they should not be put on the order paper either.
I may say I have here the total number of questions asked on orders of the day during the last session and in the first 70 days of this session. I find that in the session 1962-63, there were 1,705 questions asked on orders of the day. In the first 70 days of this session, the number is 2,941. So, if there is any question of wasting time, hon. members can draw their own conclusions. I have the statistics by parties, too, should anyone be interested in having them.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I was about to rise on a point of order and draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that the Secretary of State was in no way referring to the question of privilege raised by my hon. friend from Yukon. While I am on my feet I would once again respectfully remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State has risen seven times without having been recognized by the Chair.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN    INCOMPLETE ANSWER TO QUESTION ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I should like to say, on my question of privilege, that I am trying to co-operate with the government by putting my questions on the order paper in order to obtain information to which I feel this house and my constituents are entitled. I believe hon. members who sit on this side are entitled to do this, and the least we can expect is some kind of co-operation from the government and answers to our questions which are reasonably complete.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a traditional opportunity that is provided in the House of Commons for the bringing before the house of such matters as are of importance and deserve the consideration of the house. It is historic, it is traditional and it assures a privilege that is part and parcel of parliamentary government. It enables the house to give consideration to those matters which, in the opinion of its membership, have not been dealt with in a proper or expeditious manner. Furthermore, it enables the house, where amendments are moved, to judge the government of the day on the basis of any amendment or subamendment that may be put forward.
I know that the question of confidence is one that is being discussed today in all parts of our country and even beyond. Everywhere, not only in Canada but abroad, reference is being made to the loss of confidence not only on the part of people within our own country but beyond. Indeed, in strange places arguments are being advanced that one would not have thought possible a few months ago.
I remember so well that over the years the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) used to read with becoming modesty the editorial comment in the London Economist. That fine periodical was regarded as the voice of wisdom itself. It was quoted and requoted. I have before me the issue of the London Economist of October 19, 1963, which contains an article entitled "Ottawa's Low Ebb". It reads in part as follows:
Canada is always ripe for an argument and usually for a wrong diagnosis. Scarcely recognizable as the same place of five months ago, Ottawa gives the impression today of a rudderless mess.
I am only going to quote a few brief references. The article goes on to say:
The phrase "sixty days of decision", coined for the Pearson government, was bound to blow up in the sloganmakers* faces.
The article continues:
The tragic thing is that so much of the promise of intelligent liberalism has been lost so quickly.

Labour Relations
The ardent new frontiersmen of six months ago now admit that one more mistake, a single inadvertence, must bring the government down.
This is from an international magazine that was accepted as the gospel whenever it was critical of the former government, and it was invariably produced as a witness in support of the arguments that were then used by the Liberal party. The article goes on to refer to "the depths of insecurity and indignity that Mr. Pearson's government has so quickly plumbed after all its brave noises in April".
I recommend this article to the various ministers sitting opposite. I know they will be anxious to read it. It is interesting. It talks about the situation and says:
It began six months ago with brave ideas of running Canada on a logical, centralist economic policy-with development planning, federal pensions and municipal loans-and seemed then prepared to take on a decisive struggle for federal as against provincial power. It has taken no longer than this for the provinces to see these federal pretensions off, and with no need for a struggle after Ottawa's display of political weakness.
I look at these master men opposite and I read in the Economist these words: "Display of political weakness". The article continues:
Thick planks of Liberal policy have been shattered and the effectiveness of central government in Canada, under whatever party, has been dealt a severe blow.
The rest of it is equally good reading.

speechtext: Gloom and doom.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
I think of the change. I think of a year and a half ago when these people opposite talked about anti-Americanism and how they were going to bring about a new day. Here is what the communique said that was issued on the 11th of May, 1963 following the meeting between President Kennedy and the Prime Minister. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister said the other day that any time he wanted to call the President on the phone he could do so. Any one of us could do that. The other side of the question is that the president does not always answer. But this was not so when they met at Hyannis Port. The honeymoon is over, but they are still speaking to one another. What did the communique say?
It was agreed that both governments should always deal in a positive and co-operative manner with developments affecting their international trade and payments.
I am not going into that because I know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will be able to give the house some information in that regard.
Wise co-operation across the border can enhance rather than diminish the sovereignty of each country by making it stronger and more prosperous than before.

The Prime Minister has agreed.
On the great waters that separate and unite the two countries-the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes-it is essential that those who own and sail ships should be free to go about their lawful business without impediment or harassment.
Page Mr. Wirtz. Bring in Mr. Meany.
The Prime Minister and the President shared a common concern at the consequences that could result from industrial strife on this central waterway.
Then, come these immortal words:
The Prime Minister and the president stressed the importance of each country showing regard for the views of the other where attitudes differ. For this purpose they are arranging for more freqeur.t consultation at all levels in order that the intentions of each government may be fully appreciated by the other and misunderstanding avoided.
I am not going to go into those six misunderstandings upon which they are in complete disagreement. Then, the communique continues:
The Prime Minister and the President look forward to a period of particularly active and productive co-operation between the two countries.
What kind of co-operation has there been? What have these masterminds been able to achieve? Well, on this occasion I am going to deal with the labour situation. I begin by referring to an editorial in the Financial Post which has never been regarded as being entirely prejudiced in our favour. The editorial in the Financial Post of October 19, 1963 is entitled, "Kennedy to Meany to Hall to Banks." It reads in part as follows:
President Kennedy wants to be re-elected next year but Canadians don't like being a punching bag in his political warm-up.
Then, it says this:
But more and more the habit of pushing other people around is growing...in Washington.
I ask you to read this editorial. I am not going to read it in detail unless someone insists on having his curiosity satisfied. It says:
Take the latest example of outrageous interference-the American pressure against the Canadian government-over the labour union war on the great lakes. Belatedly, the Canadian government stepped into this mess-
This is not the same mess as was referred to in the account of the Economist; that was a mess covering everything. This is just the labour mess.
-the trustee scheme is about to be implemented. But the spectacle of the White House and the U.S. secretary of labour and whole weighty machinery of the U.S. government being gassed up to tell the Canadian government what it can and cannot do about a Canadian problem is, to say the least, unpleasant.
Now, sir, this is a most amazing change of viewpoint. A year ago, six months ago,

they said I was anti-American simply because I said Canadian policy would be determined in Canada by Canadians. This statement was ridiculed over there. I am not going to quote unless I am asked to do so, but the quotations will be complete if I am. Then, it goes on to say:
Here is the cast of characters and here is the play. Kennedy needs the labour union vote in his presidential contest next year. That means he needs the unqualified support of George Meany, the powerful head of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. To protect his hide, Meany needs all the friends he can keep and so he will do anything to please Paul Hall, the very powerful international boss of the seafarers' union.
Paul Hall, in turn, very much needs the support of Hal Banks-and the money Banks gets out of his Canadian union members.
So when the U.S. secretary of labour solemnly makes an official pilgrimage to Ottawa-
-and nobody can recall that happening before.
-and when he makes public declarations telling the Canadian government what to do, he is merely doing a chore for Kennedy who wants to do a favour for George Meany, who needs Hall, who needs the notorious Hal Banks.
From Mr. Kennedy's point of view, Canada is quite unimportant. It would, in most respects, be a lot simpler for the White House and the U.S. government if we didn't exist at all as a separate country.
Then, on October 19 there is another article in this periodical which condemned us for being anti-American because we dared to say to the United States: "We will co-operate with you; we are together facing the problem of maintaining freedom. We have done our part all over the world, but we are going to determine our policies on the basis of Canadian needs." On October 19, 1963, the Financial Post has an article captioned "White House now think Canada is just a nuisance." How has this come about? One has only needed to follow the action taken by this government in connection with the labour dispute on the great lakes to realize how uncertain has been the attitude of this government, how desirous of taking the easy course. I expected that today the Prime Minister would be announcing some action. However, we received the same reply: Tomorrow, just wait until tomorrow. When we asked him today, what are you going to do, he replies: Tomorrow. John Macdonald used to have that name, old man tomorrow.
When I asked the Prime Minister a question concerning the international longshoremen, he said he had no information. However, the telegram was sent to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) at 12.11 a.m. A summary of the telegram is this: The International Longshoremen's Union says that if the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) does
Labour Relations
not set up immediately a commission of inquiry into the pension fund, they will consider the strike settlement null and void. I point out that was the main issue of the strike, and an inquiry was promised by Judge Lippe. I asked the Prime Minister about that very serious matter and he said he had no information but would look it up. This telegram was sent to the government on Friday, at twelve noon, at a time when there is a challenge in all Canadian ports, at least most of them, to shipping.

I am not going to deal with anything other than this labour situation, because it reveals the inherent weakness of the government, diplomatic postponement, promises of action, and looking for the easy way. I repeat what I have said before, that if the government had acted early in August, and it had the support of parliament, many of today's difficulties would have been avoided. But what did the Prime Minister or his colleagues in the cabinet say?-and it must be remembered that he is the one responsible for them. They said, "We cannot do it; it is very difficult legislation." Well, we have read the trustee legislation and there is nothing very difficult in the wording or drafting of it.
If you follow the record of this government that used to tell us what it would do and how decisive it would be, you can only conclude that on the labour situation, dangerous to the economic position of our country, its record has been a syllabus of pusillanimous pussy-footing for the last several months. The members of the government have dallied on and on; they have postponed; they have been timid, but their timidity masqueraded as diplomatic definance. It has been an amazing picture.
The government decided it would ask the President of the United States for some help.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, that statement happens to be false and I ask the right hon. gentleman to accept my denial. Surely a man who has been prime minister of this country is not going to continue to repeat falsehoods in this house.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Speaking of falsity, I remember this same man who is Prime Minister today; I remember all the things he uttered both before and during the election campaign. He is the one who speaks about falsity, but the record is clear as can be when it comes to falsity. He is giving me a lecture today, but may I point out to him that the other day in this house he said, "How cheap can you get"?
He would lecture us on the proprieties. I only wish I had a copy of some of his speech on September 18,	1962, when he spoke
language that the leader of any party should not use. Yet he tries to parade as one who is just so nice. When you listen to him on the radio you would think that there but for-[DOT] you know what Churchill said about Sir Stafford Cripps.
I repeat what I have said, and it cannot be denied factually. I know it touches his finer sensibilities because after all, Mr. Speaker, you remember this magnificent document, the extracts from the joint communique to which I have just referred. You have just to look over this period of five or six months to understand why he feels annoyed.
They were going to co-operate together. Then this government plastered the United States with a 30 per cent sales tax on shares purchased externally, but it had to back down. Then members of the government went over to the United States and they were going to bring about a reduction in the amount of automobile parts imported by Canada from the United States. That was part of their policy, but again they backed down. I have read the statement which the minister made the day before yesterday, and it is quite different from what he said previously.
Then there is the labour question, and also the cancellation of an order by the United States department of defence for Canadian aircraft. All this happened in this period of a new heaven and a new earth that were going to be brought about by the change of government.
Sir, there is no help from the United States in this labour difficulty, because Mr. Kennedy needs votes. I heard that on the radio from the United States within the last few hours, and over the week end there was a meeting of labour men in western Ontario who concluded they could expect very little co-operative support from the United States in controlling this situation on the great lakes because the A.F.L.-C.I.O. is a body whose support is needed by the President of the United States.

The record has been one of worsening relations from the very beginning of the government's tenure of office. The ministers have been theorizing as to what they were going to do economically and otherwise. We have had political cackle masquerading as economic wisdom, and having to be withdrawn. That has been the record all the way along.
It is natural that, with all this running back and forth by the government, the Washington administration should think anything they would do would be acceptable. Well, what has taken place? I know how the backbenchers in the Liberal party think about it. They had a caucus the other day and I am told the private members wanted a larger voice in the government.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: They might do better.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Well it could not be made any worse.
The record in this labour situation has been frightful. Today when we asked questions, and knowing there was going to be a supply motion, the answers given us were, "We will give you full information tomorrow." Wait until tomorrow has been the promise all the way since last August. The government tried everything and finally brought the trusteeship legislation before parliament. Parliament did not hold it up. It approved the legislation almost unanimously, only four members having disagreement with some matter or other and not giving it support. The legislation was passed; but now there is further delay and the excuse has been that the government was wishing for some system to be arranged whereby the legislation, distasteful as it is, would not have to be brought into effect. Well, Mr. Meany has given his views on the whole situation. In his release he condemns what has been done in Canada. He says:
A subsequent one-man commission of inquiry appointed by the Canadian government became the vehicle for a vitriolic and vengeful attack upon the S.I.U. of Canada and its leadership.
Then he says:
In an effort to avert such legislation and to reach an acceptable solution, there have been exchanges between the A.F.L.-C.I.O., the Canadian Labour Congress, the United States secretary of labour and the Canadian ministry of labour. We have co-operated fully-
He is speaking of his organization:
-in an effort to reach agreement on a proposal whereby a voluntary joint A.F.L.-C.I.O. and C.L.C. trusteeship would be established over the seafarers international union of Canada. Such a trusteeship would have full and complete authority over the officers and operations of the union and would function with the complete support of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and its international affiliate, the S.I.U. of North America.
Labour Relations
Then he says:
These discussions failed because of disagreement on two basic issues:
The first was composition of the trusteeship. The A.F.L.-C.I.O. was prepared to accept a two-man trusteeship, one person to be designated by the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and one by the C.L.C., with the provision that in the event of any disagreement between them, the issue would be referred to a four-man committee composed of the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., the president of the Canadian Labour Congress the United States secretary of labour and the Canadian ministry of labour.
We could not get this information in this house. We have to get it from Mr. Meany in a report to his representatives across the United States. Then he goes on to say this:
The Canadian Labour Congress would not agree to this proposal. They insisted that the joint trustees turn directly to a third party in the event of a disagreement and that this third party must be a Canadian national.
Then he goes on and condemns this plan in general, and finally concludes by saying:
The A.F.L.-C.I.O. is just as opposed to the gov-erment control of unions in Canada as in Honduras or Peru or any other place on earth.
They played around with these people, and while they played our economy was in danger of being throttled. They secured a tremendous order from the U.S.S.R. It was very obvious when I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) today, when he spoke of the advice he had given two months ago to the western farmers, that he had no idea that Russia was going to be in the market for wheat. They came over here and entered into an agreement, and I think they surprised the government by their offer to purchase.
We now face a very serious situation. We ask, "What are you going to do about it?" We receive the same answer as we received in July and August. There is always an excuse; some other thing is going to be done. They got parliament to put through the legislation and then decided they would play around with it and take the easy course.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: The politically expedient course.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: That has been the course throughout. Today we face a serious, a dangerous situation. I say immediately that our attitude in this opposition throughout has been not to take political advantage of the government in this difficult matter.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING

We voted for the legislation. How much further could we go? We supported the legislation, recognizing at the same time the fact that it was legislation of a kind that should only be very temporary and that the only reason for bringing it in was the fact that there was no other course
