open. The Conservative party, as Her Majesty's loyal opposition, has in the past two or three months on this particular matter, and on other matters too-but I am speaking about labour now-done nothing to take partisan advantage of the government's action. I was glad today to have the assurance that at last they have come to a realization that this board should be Canadian. That is what we were asking for.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
They did not think that a few weeks ago, or even a few days ago. We in Her Majesty's loyal opposition will at all times support the government in any action that upholds the sovereignty of parliament and the independence of Canada against outside interference. That is the stand we took. For two years we were criticized and ridiculed by those who now occupy the treasury benches. They said, "Isn't the situation terrible? We will bring about"-and I repeat this because it was the picture put before the Canadian people-"that new heaven and that new earth". Relations with the United States were going to be the epitome of perfection. It has been a most sorry, sorry record. They were going to bring about an Atlantic union

that was the first thing they were going to do-and the New York Times says they have adopted a protectionism that will set back the Atlantic union for years to come.
These were the people who were going to co-operate and who said we were so wrong in daring to say that Canada would determine its own policies. Sir, dawdling accompanied by tranquilizing statements has been the record of this government for the last three months on this question. Their attitude has been to play around, postpone and hope that something will come up. We tried to warn them in August. Do you remember what the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) said? He said that the mere announcement of the legislation to provide a trusteeship would, he hoped, bring about peace on the great lakes. There was two months delay, giving the opposition to the government's policy time to organize. What would you expect, when the government of Canada had announced that if there was anything of a tyrannical nature on the great lakes parliament would be recalled? A Canadian ship was dynamited. Nothing was done about it. Nero fiddled while Rome burned. This government fiddled, hoping for an easy solution. They showed weakness, uncertainty.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Fumbling and bungling.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
They used to talk about bungling. I give you exhibit No. 1 in the

person of the Prime Minister. They called in American officials. Mr. Wirtz came here.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Gloom and doom.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
He tried to put pressure on Canada. I asked the Prime Minister about this, and he said, "Oh, no; the statement he made was not that". This was the first statement Wirtz made. They always took the easy way out. What was the result of all this? The result was that in the United States it was taken for granted that this was a government that could be pushed around with impunity and ease. They were pushed easily. Meany and Paul Hall were met with trepidation and timidity. You cannot blame them across the line for not taking Canada seriously. Had there been a 30-minute display of firmness at the beginning, an unmistakeable determination to act, all this would have been avoided. After all, in facing up to Hal Banks, diplomatic give and take is not one of the elements he understands as being evidence of strength.
Now what have we got? We have the promise from the Prime Minister: Wait until tomorrow. We have a situation today bordering on anarchy in Canada. Political considerations have no place here when there is anywhere in this nation a desire to supplant parliamentary legislation, right, and order on the part of any group within this country of ours. The Globe and Mail said this morning that the government had been trying to find the easy way out. It has not worked out very well. Tomorrow we shall learn what is what. It has been the same all the way along the line. Hon. gentlemen opposite have wrecked our relations with the provinces. The pension plan is now shelved. There was the budget fiasco; the auto parts which were going to be produced here in Canada. In all these things, the government has not acted. Many bulletins go out telling us what it is hoped to accomplish. What has taken place has imperilled our wheat shipments-shipments which will mean so much to the economy and to the balance of payments situation. What this government has done has caused lasting damage to our relations, economically, with the United States. I call as my witness the Canadian-American committee; and it is interesting to note that Donald Gordon was one of the signatories to a report in which it is pointed out that damage has been done to our relations by the action taken.
How has the government acted today? I was not one of those who had a visitation today. Somebody told me there was a sign carried by someone representing Prince Albert. Well, the only relationship Prince

Albert has had with the maritime scene is that the last naval battle fought in North America was fought 25 miles outside Prince Albert. Apart from that, we have no relation with what is going on in the shipping world, except in so far as the economy is directly affected. What did the Minister of Labour do? He made a statement today. It must have been produced in a great hurry because it does not contain all the decorations which are usual in such statements. It is just a simple, mimeographed record. I shall say this to the minister: I think he has tried very hard to do the very best. I do not agree with the course he has followed, but he is one who has given answers when we have asked questions of him, and that is something. He was away today, otherwise the Prime Minister would not have been answering questions and given us this indefinite answer, "tomorrow".
What was said? The federal government on October 20 ordered the seafarers international union to call off its walkout. Listen to this, for direct language:
You and the officials of your union must be aware of the fact that the directives issued in instruction bulletin No. 1 by the seaman's rights committee contravened the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act through taking illegal strike action during the term of agreement.
The government of Canada demands that you and other members of the executive board obey the law of Canada and direct all members of your union to return immediately to their ships and to resume work.
I do not know what their answer to that would be, but I do know they have had experience in the last few months.
The Minister of Justice had two outstanding lawyers look into the question of what prosecutions could take place. Mr. Justice Norris said this person should be prosecuted-referring to Banks-and the lawyers have been taking months to determine whether there could be any prosecution. First, there was a preliminary report on the subject. We asked for its production and I cannot argue with hon. gentlemen opposite when they say the document is not producible. But it shows the weakness, the temporizing, of this government. Mr. Justice Norris said grave offences had been committed by Banks. Mr. Justice Norris is a judge of wide experience at the bar. But no action was taken. Why? I do not intend to repeat the close relationship, the filial regard shown between the Liberal party and Mr. Banks. But Mr. Banks has not been prosecuted, unless, tomorrow, we are told so after this motion has been dealt with.
The minister was asked: "What are you going to do?" I am reading from the article in the Globe and Mail by Bernard Dufresne:
Labour Relations
Asked what would happen if Mr. Banks does not order his membership to return to work, Mr. MacEachen said with a short chuckle: "We'll have to wait and see. There are a number of sanctions that may be taken by the companies and the government."
This is the kind of decisiveness we have had-chuckles and postponements. Today, the Prime Minister says: Wait until tomorrow. This must have put the fear of retribution into the hearts of all those who have read it today. They gathered here on parliament hill. A Canadian citizen has a right to bring his views to the attention of parliament. This right has existed as far back as 1623 or 1624-the right of petition. They gathered here, and the minister made a statement. It reads as follows:
You have been told that the new trusteeship law will harm you, your jobs and your unions. This is a false statement. Unions often establish their own trusteeships. It was hoped this could be done in the present situation. When this proved impossible, government action had to be taken.
It goes on to mention the powers of the trustees and what rights the unions have. Then it says:
The members of the maritime transportation unions are asked to co-operate fully with the trustees in carrying out their responsibilities.
Tomorrow's sun never yet rose or set on any human being. Tomorrow, there is to be action, the Prime Minister said. Think of all the tomorrows that have gone by since July 25. This has been a history of indecision, confusion and uncertainty. On August 2, as reported at page 2943 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
It would be impossible in the circumstances to have this difficult and complicated legislation prepared within a matter of weeks. It may require a strict examination of the constitutionality of the legislation, and it might mean getting in touch with the provincial governments concerned-
An examination of that bill reveals little of those elements of complexity or consultative difficulty which were referred to. A little further on he said:
I hope very much that the indication that this legislation is being prepared and will be made effective will hold the situation during the summer.
Well, "tomorrow" came with the dynamiting of the Howard L. Shaw, a Canadian ship.
At the same page in Hansard I asked the Prime Minister, regarding this report which was released on July 18:
-would the Prime Minister give consideration to bringing before the house before the adjournment the legislation to which reference was made yesterday.. .Otherwise there may well be an invitation to further lawlessness and disorder and a tie-up of shipping-

Labour Relations
But no; the reply was that the next day the house would adjourn and we would come back it there was any trouble.
On September 30 the Minister of Labour said, as reported at page 3026 of Hansard:
-I think I should tell the house in all fairness that I have some faint hope that if we get a break in the next short time we may be in a different position in several days, but at the moment the decision is to proceed at the earliest possible opportunity, having given the necessary notice, with the trusteeship legislation.
Again that tortuous uncertainty, that postponement, that waffling; that is what it has been all the way along throughout the entire course. Today I thought we would get an answer. On October 3 the Minister of Labour said, as reported at page 3150 of Hansard:
I can assure the hon. member that our purpose in this situation is to establish an effective alternative if possible.
Negotiations were going on. Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that all these peregrinations back and forth were calculated to impress the United States with the government's intention and determination to go ahead with the Norris recommendations? They brought Mr. Reynolds to Canada, as the Minister of Labour said, as a result of a request made to the secretary of labour in the United States. Mr. Wirtz came to Canada on September 11 to express his opposition, and Mr. Reynolds gave his views later on. It is just impossible to understand what has taken place. I suppose that only history will reveal everything that took place.
Under all the circumstances, therefore, I think it is clear that I intend to move an amendment-not wait until tomorrow, although welcoming, as we do at last, an attitude of action on the part of this government, rather than one of putting off, waffling, postponing, and using the phone, even though not answered. It is today when we are in parliament. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This government, because of its confusion, inconsistency and pusillanimous dawdling and delays in taking effective action has encouraged chaos approaching anarchy to develop on the great lakes, the seaway, and in several Canadian ports, thereby causing disruption in shipping and the placing in jeopardy of essential trade in general, and in particular contracts for delivery of wheat to foreign countries."

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this afternoon in moving his non-confidence motion, which has already been put on the record with its interesting adjectives, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) told us he was going to deal with the labour situation, which is admittedly now difficult in some aspects and could, I admit, become dangerous. The successful effort to restore communications with our neighbour, the United States, which had been completely broken by the end of the last regime, was sneered at. I recall that the joint defence committee had not met for a very long time under the previous administration, that the trade and economic committee had practically ceased to function, and that the heads of government in the two countries had not communicated with each other. The right hon. gentleman seems unable to conceal his chagrin that all this has now changed.
He is very worried because of my alleged difficulties in getting the President of the United States on the telephone. This really seems to disturb him. subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING

It is deplorable when that happens in the relations between our two governments and our two countries, and even more deplorable when a senior member of his party has to descend to the depths that have been descended to in putting a forged communication on the record in order to stir up trouble between our two countries. We are going to have enough difficulty in the days and weeks and months ahead in solving the problems that face our two countries without adding to that difficulty by that kind of tactic.

Let us have a look at the position both in respect of what this government has tried to do-

They were all willing but one. The egg was 95 per cent fresh.
Then, the right hon. gentleman sneered at the argument put forward by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) and others that a certain time was required to make sure that the legislation as drafted would stand up in the courts; would be perfectly sound from every point of view, and especially from a constitutional point of view. If the right hon. gentleman thinks, as he professes to think, that the drafting of this legislation was a simple matter which could have been worked out in a day or two, he does not know anything about its complexity. I wish very much he could submit this question to a committee, have the officials of the Department of Justice brought before this committee where they could be examined on the difficulties in drafting this kind of legislation, on the difficulties in making sure that what we put before this parliament would not conflict with provincial jurisdiction in the field of property and civil rights.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we had also to relate this particular legislation to my hon. friend's pet piece of legislation, the bill of rights. Also a great many union contracts had to be examined very carefully to make sure that the trusteeship set up, if it had to be set up by the government, would have sufficient power to do the thing that had to be done, that is clean up the situation in this union as it was disclosed in the Norris report and in accordance with certain Norris recommendations. Quite rightly, therefore, we took the necessary time to make sure that the legislation was sound.
While this legislation was being drafted, and it took a few weeks to get this done in the right way, we then proceeded to see if there were some satisfactory alternative to the government having to take this power and establish, what I think most hon. members will consider to be, an undesirable precedent. The right hon. gentleman would not have done that. He would not have sought any other alternative. He would have plunged right in with government trusteeship, irrespective of the wishes of everybody, including the Canadian Labour Congress. While the legislation was being drafted, indeed while the legislation was going through the house, the government had established through the Minister of Labour, whose work I think in this matter is to be commended, the closest possible co-operation with the Canadian

Labour Congress and maintained that cooperation right up until this moment. This co-operation would have been abandoned by the right hon. gentleman if he had his way, because he would have rushed in at once, without any delay, into government trusteeship, irrespective of the wishes of the Canadian Labour Congress.

He would have insisted on public trusteeship at once. Never mind the necessity for care, but rush in. He would have said: Never mind whether there could be a better alternative than public trusteeship; let the government charge ahead and take over these labour unions. Never mind whether there is any hope of agreeing on a private solution with the approval of the Canadian Labour Congress, but rush ahead. Never mind what the consequences are in Canada, and never mind the consequences in relation to the United States.
Well, Mr. Speaker, this government rejected that course and we are glad that we did. We worked with the Canadian Labour Congress, we encouraged them and supported them in every way we could in getting in touch with the A.F.L.-C.I.O. in the United States.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Did you get in touch with Mr. Wirtz?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has made a great play about the fact we on this side of the line, through the C.L.C., and indeed through the government, got in touch with the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and the government of the United States in respect of a matter which was basically Canadian, but which had very important and dangerous international implications.
The right hon. gentleman does not mind that. He would rush ahead-"damn the torpedoes"-straight ahead with legislation. We thought it was better to see if we could
Labour Relations
work out through negotiations between the Canadian Labour Congress and the A.F.L.-C.I.O., with the support of the United States government and the Canadian government, a private trusteeship which would be satisfactory from the Canadian viewpoint and which would make unnecessary government intervention in this matter.
From the very beginning the Canadian Labour Congress and the Canadian government insisted that no such private trusteeship would be satisfactory unless two out of the three trustees were Canadians. The right hon. gentleman made great play with the fact that for the first time this afternoon he learned that in a public trusteeship we were going to have three Canadians. This was a remarkable discovery on his part, that a Canadian government public trusteeship was to have three Canadians.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there never was any question in anybody's mind that in a public trusteeship the three trustees would have to be Canadians; but in a private trusteeship, if it were to be effective for maintaining and securing peace on the great lakes on the American side, in our view it was not too high a price to pay for that through an agreement which would make it possible, to have one of the three trustees a United States citizen. If, as a result of that kind of trusteeship with that kind of membership, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. could give us an assurance that Canadian ships, manned by Canadian seamen under this kind of trusteeship arrangement, would not be interfered with on the great lakes and in American ports, surely that was not too high a price to pay for that kind of agreed arrangement between the two labour organizations of the two countries.
That is what we tried to bring about, and in all these negotiations the Canadian Labour Congress was clear, and we were clear, that two of the three trustees had to be Canadians. In the first stages that was one of the reasons that the negotiations broke down.
Another condition we laid down from the beginning was that a private trusteeship must have sufficient authority to clean up the S.I.U. in Canada. There could be no question about that. It must have sufficient authority to do the job that was required to be done whether by a government trusteeship or a private trusteeship, in accordance with certain recommendations of the Norris report.
The negotiations became very difficult. They became almost impossible when the head of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., Mr. Meany, made what has been described by many hon. members inside the house, and outside the house, as a shocking statement which represented complete ignorance of Canadian affairs and a shocking intervention in Canadian affairs. If it were

Labour Relations
done entirely through ignorance perhaps he is not as open to condemnation as it it were done by calculation, but in any event it was a mischievous intervention which made it extremely difficult to make any progress.
Mr. Wirtz, the secretary of labour, who had been working hard and conscientiously to bring about a kind of meeting of minds with his opposite number, the Minister of Labour, so that a private trusteeship would be agreeable to both countries, then made what I described as an unhelpful intervention-and it certainly was-but it was not designed to be harmful or deliberately mischievous. In any event, the negotiations were on the point of breaking down on this issue of membership after the intervention of Mr. Meany, which in a sense was an incitement to disobey any trusteeship. So, in those circumstances I thought it might be useful if I got in touch with the President of the United States and asked for his intervention, to see if we could get negotiations restored on the only basis where there was possibility of success, namely that there should be a clear understanding about the composition of a private trusteeship and about its authority and powers.
This afternoon the right hon. gentleman said the president was not helpful in this matter. I would say that we got a great deal more help from the President of the United States in this matter than we got from the right hon. gentleman who, day after day, kept demanding details of the negotiations while negotiations were going on, knowing perfectly well that if you give the details of your negotiation in the middle of negotiations you have much less chance of coming to a successful agreement. But that did not deter the right hon. gentleman from trying to probe for details such as, "How many times did you phone the president; how quickly did he answer the phone"? And the right hon. gentleman got so upset over the allegation that somehow or other President Kennedy did not answer the phone quickly enough that it moved him to national indignation.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: They tell me the Prime Minister was awfully annoyed, too, when he did not answer.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
As a result of President Kennedy's intervention and my talk with him, the negotiations were resumed. They were resumed in good faith by the Canadian Labour Congress, and with the support and the approval of the government. They were resumed in the hope that we could-even at that late time when the bill had passed the House of Commons, was going to the Senate and would shortly be given royal assent- work out a private trusteeship before the

legislation was proclaimed, a private trusteeship which would clean up the conditions exposed by the Norris report in the S.I.U. of Canada, a branch of an international union, something which gave the international headquarters in the United States some standing on the matter; and second, an arrangement which would receive the formal support of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. and which would ensure that Canadian shipping in United States lake ports would not be interfered with or harassed.
While these resumed negotiations were proceeding and encouraging progress was being made, Mr. Hal Banks ordered from their ships members of his union, and organized the march on Ottawa which took place today. The first act, Mr. Speaker, was illegal, and the second-notwithstanding what the right hon. gentleman said about it this afternoon as a vindication of the historic rights of the citizen to petition his member of parliament- I believe was an effort to bring unjustifiable pressure on the government with respect to legislation which had passed through this house and the Senate, and had received the royal assent.
In the face of this illegal action the Canadian Labour Congress decided yesterday that it was useless, and indeed from their point of view improper, to continue negotiations. The government understands and supports the position which they took.
We have done everything we can on this side to make unnecessary a public trusteeship over Canadian unions through legislation. We had hoped, Mr. Speaker, that this could have been avoided by satisfactory private arrangements. The illegal action taken by Mr. Hal Banks and the S.I.U., and the refusal of the
S.I.U. international in the United States to do anything to prevent this-as they could have done because they knew what was happening-leaves the government with no alternative but to proceed without delay to proclaim the act putting the public trusteeship into effect, and this is what we propose to do.

speechtext: When?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: We propose to do this far more quickly than was the case with my hon. friends opposite, when they took any action in respect of any situation.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: We must show that Canada, and free and responsible trade unionism in Canada, is bigger than Mr. Banks-

speechtext: When?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
-and that a Canadian government is not going to be intimidated by the

illegal action and pressure of one who has destroyed democratic government in his own union. This morning, Mr. Speaker-the prime minister is going to be very disappointed about this-I rang up the White House again and I got through-

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: The prime minister is going to be disappointed?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wanted to make the right hon. gentleman feel a little better. As long as he pursues the kind of tactics that he pursued this afternoon, in the face of a dangerous national situation, he is going to be over on that side for a long, long, long time.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Therefore I think it is only fair once in a while to remind him that he was once prime minister. I telephoned the President this morning-he had the secretary of labour with him at the White House-and told him that the illegal and, as I thought it was, provocative action that was going on in Ottawa at the moment I was telephoning made it quite impossible for the Canadian Labour Congress to continue in negotiation with the A.F.L.-C.I.O. about a private trusteeship. I added that I thought this was particularly unfortunate because those negotiations had been so close to agreement.
I told the president we were distressed by recent developments but that we must support the position, and we would support the position, taken by the Canadian Labour Congress. They could not be expected to discuss matters in the face of this kind of pressure, and therefore the government had no alternative now but to proclaim its legislation putting a public trusteeship into effect.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING

We have had a demonstration today in Ottawa. I believe that a good many of those who were here have some misunderstanding about the nature of the legislation

Labour Relations
and the effect it will have on trade unions in Canada. We as members of parliament have done what we can on this side, in the interviews we have had with the delegates of the demonstration, to correct some of the misunderstandings and remove some of the misapprehension that is obviously in the minds of certain of the members of the S.I.U. who came to Ottawa.
They have been told by their leadership that the new trusteeship law will harm them, harm their jobs and harm their union. That is a false statement. The new law will protect seamen and their unions by seeking to ensure that union affairs are conducted honestly and decently. Seamen are protected under the new law from any high handed action which interferes with their democratic rights either from within or from outside their unions. The trustees to be named under the legislation are required, (1) to protect the funds and property of the unions from being misused; (2) to recommend changes in the constitutions and bylaws of the unions, which will ensure democratic control of the unions by their members, and no such changes can be made without the approval of the members; (3) the trustees are required to establish advisory committees of seamen and, where necessary, bargaining committees. They are required to establish means whereby union members may manage their affairs efficiently and democratically. Members of the unions concerned have nothing to fear from the trusteeship imposed under this legislation.
The act has been passed by parliament and has been given the royal assent. When it is proclaimed and in effect, it will have the constructive purpose of cleaning up a particular union, and in due course and as soon as possible return the unions to their members. I am sure the trustees will serve the best interests of the members and their unions and that the members, the seamen, will have every opportunity to be heard. Any just grievance will be considered by the trustees. Under the legislation the unions will not lose their rights to bargain or to strike. Surely this should at least help to remove some of the misunderstanding and misapprehension that has been caused by the information given to members by officers of the union. It should even, I hope, remove some of the wilder misunderstanding existing across the line in some union circles as to what we are doing in Canada about a Canadian union. If that misunderstanding can be removed, then I believe this trusteeship legislation will be acceptable to all union members in Canada -all union members-and it will help to restore peace on the great lakes.
I would have preferred, as I think most of those in this house would have preferred, to

have had a private arrangement. That was impossible. Therefore we have proceeded with our legislation. We believe that in the way we have produced this legislation, in the effort we have made to find a suitable alternative, and the way we have worked from beginning to end with the Canadian Labour Congress, we have followed the right course as a responsible government.

Mr. Speaker, now that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) have berated each other and covered a good deal of territory in their respective speeches, I should like to draw the attention of the house for a few minutes to the amendment itself.
This amendment which the Leader of the Opposition has moved criticizes the government for its dawdling and delay in taking effective action as a result of which, it says, there has been disruption of shipping and the placing in jeopardy of the trade of this country, in particular of deliveries of wheat to foreign ports. I should like to begin by saying that members in all parts of the house are naturally concerned that nothing should happen which would interrupt the promised deliveries of wheat to countries which are Canadian customers. This concern is not felt by the Conservative party alone. It is felt, I think, by members in all parties. As a matter of fact, shipping has not yet been hurt. I shall have something to say about what the future holds a little later in my observations. But, so far, this temporary stoppage has not affected wheat shipments or trade in general as the amendment suggests.
What interested me most in the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition was that though he berated the government for its failure to act, I could find nothing in his remarks which indicated what he wanted them to do. Day after day I have listened to members of the official opposition calling upon the government to do something without saying specifically what it was they wanted the government to do. This is a very happy position to take because then, no matter what they do, they are able to criticize. The Leader of the Opposition is critical because the government has not acted promptly to implement the recommendations of the Norris report. But I need hardly remind the house that the situation on the great lakes did not spring up over night. This has been a most unfortunate and lamentable situation which has existed over a period of years. The S.I.U. were put out of the Canadian Labour Congress, if I remember correctly, as far back as 1959; and in May of 1962 the president of the C.L.C. wrote to the present

Leader of the Opposition, who was then prime minister, setting out in detail certain acts of intimidation, violence and lawlessness and urging that immediate steps should be taken to rectify the situation. Weeks passed and nothing was done. It was only when the Canadian labour movement tied up the St. Lawrence seaway that a commissioner was finally appointed in July, 1962. So, when the Leader of the Opposition calls for action, I for one, would be interested to know what specific action he has in mind. Certainly, there was no very specific action taken in those years from 1959 to 1962.
Let me say a word about the delay which has occurred with respect to appointing a board of public trustees to take over the maritime shipping unions. I think the government was justified in taking time to do two very important things. The first was to explore the possibility of setting up a private trusteeship. I am sure no member of this house, particularly those who have a great respect for free trade unions, wants to see a government trusteeship imposed on any union or group of unions. It seems to me the government was justified in taking whatever time was necessary, within reason, to explore the possibility of a private trusteeship in which trade union leaders responsible to the labour movement in Canada would be charged with trying to rectify the situation on the great lakes.
There was another advantage attached to the setting up of a private trusteeship, if it could have been arranged, namely that it might have secured the co-operation of the United States labour organization, the A.F.L.-C.I.O. This is important because everyone knows that much of our trade on the great lakes is in the United States ports, and if Canadian ships are to be handled expeditiously great value must be attached to having the full co-operation of the United States labour movement. My feeling has been that the government should have explored with the Canadian and United States labour movements the possibility of a private trusteeship which would have brought the five maritime unions under its control and sought to settle the difficulties which have disturbed the shipping industry for the past four years.
I think there is some evidence that the government has been doing just that. That is the first thing they needed to do, and I cannot blame them for taking time to do it.
The second thing they needed time to do was to look very carefully for the right kind of men to serve on the board of trustees. Merely setting up a board of trustees will not effectively deal with this problem. What will count is the way in which the board operates 28902-5-244J
Labour Relations
-whether it shows intelligence, firmness and sympathy in dealing with these unions. This trusteeship could be a farce and a failure if the right kind of men are not vested with the great authority which parliament has given. If the government needed some time to canvass the situation in order to get the right kind of men for this job, I, for one, am prepared to see that they get the necessary time. I wish to urge, once again, that those appointed to this board will include at least one, and perhaps two men with a wide experience of the trade union movement- men who are not involved in this dispute, but men who know how to lead unions back into a democratic way of doing business, so that they can emerge from this trusteeship strong, democratic and effective.
Having said that I am not prepared to criticize the government because it was seeking an alternative course of a private trusteeship, and because it has taken some time to canvass the situation and get the right kind of personnel for the board of trustees, let me say that I think the test of the government's courage and decisiveness will now lie in what they do in the next day or two. If this withdrawal of men from the ships over the last 48 hours were to continue it could pose a very serious problem for the shipment of goods, and particularly for the shipment of wheat. This is one of the things upon which our economy is depending for a large amount of money to help balance our international payments.
It was perfectly clear from the statement which was made yesterday by Mr. Claude Jodoin, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, that all attempts at setting up a private trusteeship had failed. I need not go into the details of why they failed; certainly the S.I.U. in calling the men off the ships in my opinion made it much more difficult to proceed with a private trusteeship. A private trusteeship established in the face of intimidation and threats would have been a private trusteeship that would be weakened from the very beginning of its operations. I can quite understand why the Canadian labour movement came to the conclusion that in this situation, with an illegal strike and an illegal walk-off confronting them, they could not see any way in which a private trusteeship could operate successfully. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I think one is safe in assuming that all efforts to establish a private trusteeship have failed.
It seems to me that it is now for the government to act promptly and decisively. I think the government has no choice now but to proclaim the legislation and to set up the public trusteeship just as expeditiously as possible. Indeed, I would go one step further.

If the walk-out of the seamen continues, or if there is any evidence that the companies are seeking to embarrass the trusteeship, then the government may have to take further steps. It is rather significant that in the last two or three days men have been able to walk off ships in some instances with the consent of the company, which under the Canada Shipping Act they are required to get from the master of the ship. This leads me to wonder whether or not there is collusion in this instance with the shipping companies, whether or not they too are seeking to intimidate the government and parliament. They may also enter into arrangements which would intimidate the board of trustees. I think the government has to give serious consideration to doing what was done, if I remember correctly, in 1946 when a government controller of shipping was set up. Because unless the board of trustees can get the wholehearted co-operation of the companies as well as the trade unions, then the board of trustees cannot possibly hope to operate with any great degree of success.
I think the government has to deal promptly and aggressively in this matter. Let us just see what has happened in the last 48 hours. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen) informed the S.I.U. by telegram, according to the press, that this walk-off from the ships constituted an illegal strike, and ordered the men to go back to work. Yet when the member for Winnipeg North asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) this afternoon what he proposed to do about it, he said that if these men have broken the law the responsibility lies with the shipping companies to deal with them. This is not decisive action. For the Minister of Labour to say that this strike is illegal and that the men must go back to work, and for the Minister of Justice to wash his hands of it and say that this is not his responsibility, but that it is up to the shipping companies to act if the seamen have broken their collective agreements and violated the Canada Shipping Act, does not indicate the kind of decisiveness which is going to be needed in the next few days if the trusteeship is going to operate successfully.
I feel that the government should proclaim the legislation. I believe they should set up the board of trustees just as quickly as they can find the right personnel. One of the first things which must be done is to get the necessary information to the members of these unions, and particularly to the S.I.U., making it clear what are the purposes of the trusteeship. I was glad the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) indicated in his remarks some of the things the board of trustees would do. Many of the men who were out in front

of the parliament buildings today are genuinely concerned. They have not been given the facts of the case. Some of them fear that they will lose their jobs when the trusteeship comes in. It should be made clear to them by the trustees and the government that they will have job security; that there will be no interference with seniority. One of the functions of a board of trustees will be to go into the company records and establish seniority for these men. These men are afraid that there will not be proper collective bargaining; that the trusteeship will be able to sit down and negotiate any collective bargaining agreement it likes and the men will have to live with it, and that consequently their wages, fringe benefits and their standard of living will be reduced. What the Prime Minister said tonight needs to be emphasized, not just in a speech in the House of Commons but in material sent out to the individual members, namely that these men will still have the right to bargain collectively through their own selected negotiating committees; that they will still have the right to strike legally, provided they comply with the laws of the country; that they will lose none of the rights of a democratic trade union but that, on the contrary, the purpose of the trusteeship is to restore to them the democracy which, in at least one instance, has been taken away from them.
I should like to say to the government that we in the New Democratic party have supported the legislation for setting up a government trusteeship. But I also want to warn the government that we will expect them to make it clear to the trustees that the basic rights of the workers of these five labour unions must be safeguarded and protected. We will consider it one of our tasks in this house to ask questions and raise issues whenever we think this trusteeship is not conducting the affairs of these unions in a democratic and proper manner. The one thing these men do not want is the substitution of one dictatorship for another. What they want, and what I believe they will accept, is a trusteeship designed to act in their best interests, one which will restore to them at the earliest possible date the full democratic rights which every free trade union in a free nation has the right to enjoy.
Neither this house nor the government, Mr. Speaker, need think that by appointing a board of trustees the whole problem will be settled. The government and the board of trustees will have to get the co-operation and confidence of the men. This is my first plea, that everything be done to work with them and to make it clear to them that this trusteeship is not something which is being

The other place where the government will have a great responsibility is in endeavouring to secure the co-operation of the government of the United States, which I hope in turn can secure the co-operation of the United States labour movement, to see to it that Canadian ships in United States ports will be free from harassment and sabotage. This is one of the things that a private trusteeship might have had great difficulty in doing, but at government level the government should be able to exercise all its powers of persuasiveness and representation on the American government, so that Canadian ships manned by whatever seamen and by whatever union can get proper access to American ports, and the rights that they should have in those ports.
May I sum up by saying I do not share the view that the government has dawdled in the matter of dealing with the Norris report. I think that up until now they have taken the wise course of examining and exploring every alternative in the hope that it might not be necessary to take this very radical and far reaching step. But I urge the government now, when all hope of a private trusteeship is gone, not to hesitate any longer but to act decisively and, above all, to act humanely in the interests of the workers concerned.

Mr. Speaker, when you read the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), you wonder, with good reason, if his parliamentary advisers did their work well. I wonder, in view of the chaos and strife that prevail on the great lakes at the present time, if it is in order-even though the parliamentary procedure allows it-to move an amendment written in such terms?
In my opinion that amendment is not at all in the interest of those who are waiting for us to take action, because all of us without exception in this house have declared ourselves in favor of a settlement by the private companies which deal with the interested unions.
Everyone would have preferred to see the matter settled directly by the employers and the unions in the great lakes area, and if we waited until the last moment, it is because the government was forced to intervene at the request of all members in the house and various Canadian unions.
As a matter of fact, what does the amendment say? I quote:

This government, because of its confusion, inconsistency and pusillanimous dawdling and delays in taking effective action has encouraged chaos approaching anarchy to develop on the great lakes, the seaway, and in several Canadian ports, thereby causing disruption in shipping and the placing in
(Mr. Olson.]
jeopardy of essential trade in general, and in particular contracts for delivery of wheat to foreign countries.

Mr. Speaker, we sincerely believe that the present situation did not arise only yesterday or a couple of weeks ago. The trouble already existed between unions and employers and even between the unions themselves on the great lakes. This situation existed when the Conservatives were in office and even before. I find it hard to understand today that such an amendment which blames the government for taking action according to a request to that effect made by the different parties of the house and the unions themselves, should be entertained. I am neither Liberal nor Conservative, but, in my opinion, under the circumstances, we must show some intelligence, and in this case, we have no alternative but to yield to evidence and support the government.
The government waited till the last moment to take action, hoping that the matter would be settled between employers and labour or between the unions themselves.
A dispute arose between American and Canadian unions. Street fights broke out in some towns near the great lakes between members of Canadian and American unions.
However, there is a point on which I insist strongly: the government should see by all possible and conceivable means, that our Canadian unions are subject to no interference from federal and provincial governments in the disputes between employers and employees.
It is not within the province of the government to take the place of the employers, or of the employees or of the unions. The government is merely authorized to ensure good relations between these various groups of our society.
We, of the Social Credit, honestly believe that in this dispute the government is acting the way it should, and in my opinion, the amendment moved by the opposition is neither timely nor wise, and our group will certainly not support it, for this very serious conflict prevailing on the great lakes must be settled in the nearest possible future.

Tonight, Mr. Speaker, I shall follow the example of some of the previous speakers and try to be as brief as possible. The amendment charges the government with inconsistency, delays and lack of policy. I think that such an amendment is well founded, and for proof of that one only needs to scan the record of the present administration since it took office. I know that when the

much vaunted 60 days of action turned out to be a somewhat less brilliant success than anticipated, some people said that might be understandable. After all, a government must be given time. They have to adapt themselves. They have to acquire the managerial skills. Give them time, and they will prove themselves.
Well, they have had the time. They have had their 60 days and they have had at least 60 days of grace. The recent recess should have been a period of sober second thoughts for the government. Many people thought the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and members of his cabinet would develop those imaginative policies about which the Prime Minister spoke so fluently during his last days in opposition, and during the election campaign, out of which would emerge sound government policies. The Liberal party convinced the people of Canada that they were the only ones who could provide sound government for this country. After those 60 days, Mr. Speaker, and after all that followed those 60 days, I defy the Prime Minister, any member of his cabinet or any member sitting over there to say truthfully that the end result of the new administration has not been a profound disappointment for them. This government has been proven, across the length and breadth of this country, to be amateurish and it has done wrong in practically every field of endeavour into which it has ventured.
I might be accused of speaking in generalities, so it may be a good thing for me to get down to specifics, and one of these specifics is precisely the subject of this amendment. The amendment deals with Canadian-Ameri-can relations and, Mr. Speaker, if there were any field in which the Canadian people sincerely believed that, by handing over the reins of government to the present Prime Minister and administration, there would be an improvement, it was in that field.
A few months ago the Prime Minister said that during the tenure of office of the previous administration relations between Canada and the United States had been permitted to deteriorate. That is what he said; and he played a leading part last February in bringing about the fall of the previous government. He participated in a debate in this house on February 5, 1963, and as recorded at page 3454 of Hansard for that date he said:
We want to get back to those days when Canada was so respected, because she did make her own policy.
What has happened since then? The Canadian government is not making its own policy now. It is not making its own international policy in spheres which involve the United States government, and we all know
Labour Relations
the interference that we have had from that quarter. It is admitted by everyone. For example, the Prime Minister himself said that the interference of Mr. Meany was shocking, but much more grave to my mind was the interference of secretary of labour Wirtz, which the Prime Minister has branded in perhaps the understatement of the year as being less than helpful.
Well, Mr. Speaker, under this weak, hesitant government we do not make our own policies these days. We are not respected because we are not making our own policies. Last February the Prime Minister said that if he assumed office Canada would make her own policies in co-operation and friendship with her allies, but we know the results today. Not only do we not make our own policies with our neighbours, but the government cannot even make up its mind and cannot evolve constructive and definite policies. I defy anyone sitting on the government benches to point out any government in recent times which has backed down more often than the present government from its announced measures both in the budget, in resolutions and in proposed legislation.
Indeed, in modern times there has never been a weaker government in Canada, and one has to go back to the weak Liberal government of Alexander Mackenzie in 1873, almost a century ago, to find a parallel. We all know what happened to that Mackenzie government and how long it took the Liberal party to regain power.
Mr. Speaker, I had intended to be brief but the subject matter flows so abundantly, the examples are so numerous and the mistakes so fantastic that I can hardly pass up this opportunity to review them. I shall deal with but a few and, if I may so express myself, I am only scratching the surface. The Prime Minister laughs, but I would point out that according to a story carried by the Canadian Press and reported in the Ottawa Journal of October 11, 1963, it is stated:
Canada-U.S. ties strained in 1963. Not-so-friendly neighbours.
Does the Prime Minister really think that this is a laughing matter-a laughing matter for this House of Commons or a laughing matter for the Canadian people? This article is substantiated by a large number of cases in point, all of them uncontroverted, and it refers to the unthinkable, almost incredible blunders of the Minister of Finance in the course of his budget legislation. There was the take-over securities tax from which the government sheepishly withdrew. Was that an example of the sound, constructive leadership which we were led to expect?

Second, I believe it is very pertinent to this debate, because the debate deals with Canada-American relations, and the rate of our dollar in relation to the American dollar is very pertinent to those relations. However,
I shall go on to another subject, because I understand how little government members want to hear about the dollar.
I was referring to articles such as the one I mentioned a moment ago, articles which are being published in periodicals all over the country, articles such as the one in the Economist to which the Leader of the Opposition referred this afternoon. They all show how much the government has lost its touch. How far away in the dim and vague past is the subtle hand of the great diplomat who now occupies the elevated position of Prime Minister of Canada. Where is the astute diplomat now?

speechtext: Right here.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
Only a few days ago there was another article in the Ottawa Journal on U.S.-Canada relations, written by I. Norman Smith, and headed "Stuntsmanship is not Statesmanship." I hope the Prime Minister and the members of his government have read that article, and that they realize how publicity stunts have recently led to a deterioration of these relations. Perhaps he will take the advice proffered in that article to go back to the ordinary fields of consultation between foreign experts and diplomats of both countries, and thus restore that free, easy and friendly relationship that should exist between Canada and our great neighbour to the south. That is what we in Canada want, but unfortunately that is not what we have received from the government.
In this matter of trusteeship legislation a lot of weakness has been displayed by the government. First we had a report by Mr. Justice Norris that revealed the shocking conditions existing on the great lakes, disruption of shipping, gangsterism, and all the excesses that are brought about by violence and disdain for the law. That was clear enough. Mr. Speaker, that report was brought in. The situation was defined as being urgent,

but the government decided to wait. When it received the report, it acted as if it had received a baby from someone else, and it was a most embarrassing thing. It was a package which they did not want to touch.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Don't you like babies?

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: I like babies, but I also like a government that acts with a bit of decisiveness. The conduct of the government and the whole course of its decisions pertaining to this trusteeship legislation has displayed once again its lack of policy, its lack of decisiveness. The other opposition parties may think the government has acted in the right way.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ADEQUATELY WITH DISRUPTION OF GREAT LAKES SHIPPING
speechtext:
I admit that before placing Canadian unions under trusteeship every other avenue had to be explored. But I think too much time was spent-and I charge the government with this failure-not in sound negotiation, but simply in wishful thinking, in the hope that something would turn up. That something has not turned up and we have had these delays. First there was the delay in receiving the report, second in deciding to do anything about the report, third in implementing the legislation, and now in proclaiming the legislation. Then we had today's demonstration which, according to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), was illegal because it was a walkout which in fact constituted a strike, and a strike that could not be justified under the seamen's contracts and under existing law; and the Prime Minister said the very fact of the march upon Ottawa was a way of exerting undue pressure on the government. The Prime Minister knows and the government know-or they should-that this walkout, coupled with the strike of the longshoremen that caused costly and very serious delays in the delivery of grain shipments to Russia and other countries, is placing our economy in jeopardy; yet they have done nothing up to this time.
The Prime Minister was asked today whether any sanctions would be taken against the union boss and members of the union for their illegal action, for their violation of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, and he said he will consider that matter. This is as far as they have progressed in this regard. Despite what the other opposition parties may say, is it not logical, is it not almost imperative that the opposition raise this question by proposing the motion of non-confidence which it has proposed? We must do this because it is our role to make the government realize it has mishandled this issue very badly and has completely mishandled the very important, vital question

of our relationship with the United States. Our only purpose in bringing this motion forward is to expose that indecision and inconsistency, and to express the hope that some action will be taken and that now the act will be proclaimed.
The Prime Minister said it would be proclaimed tomorrow. I hope it is proclaimed tomorrow. I hope, also, that the trustees will be appointed tomorrow; that the government will not allow unbearable pressure to be exerted upon it in regard to the proclamation and the execution of the provisions of the legislation and the appointment of the trustees. If the past record is any indication, I am afraid there will be further delay and there might also be more backtracking. Having regard to all these circumstances, to the sorry, disappointing performance of the government in every field, particularly in the very vital field of Canada-United States relations, to its hesitancy in permitting a very serious situation in the disruption of shipping to continue and to be aggravated, I think the government can no longer enjoy the confidence of this house. Those at the far end of this side of the house who on past occasions, when embarrassing questions have been raised, have abstained from voting, should support this motion. Surely, also, the Social Credit party, be it one group or another-those who say they are in favour of free enterprise, of democratic rights and all the rest-should also be the first to support this motion, because I know it is supported by the facts and by a large body of public opinion across this land.

Mr. Speaker, it does seem to be necessary to prolong the debate on the motion put by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). I would think that to every reasonable, thinking member of this house the putting of a motion of this kind amply points out the utter futility that must 28902-5-245
Labour Relations
be rampant in the opposition benches. It points out two prominent phenomena, to my mind, after listening to the Leader of the Opposition. First, it does seem strange that this non-confidence motion is based on a criticism of the government's handling of the labour strike and the S.I.U. It seems so strange because very influential and diverse components in our society-and I might say, opposing components in our society-such as the labour movement on the one hand and certainly the business interests on the other hand, seem to unanimously approve the government's action in this regard. Therefore it seems strange that on an issue such as this, where the government is to a great degree obtaining support from all walks of life and even from opposing groups in regard to this issue, it should be this issue upon which the opposition desires to bring down the government. To my way of thinking it indicates just how desperate is the opposition to find an issue at this stage. It certainly points out what a fantastic waste of time there is in this parliament when we have sunk to the level of debating frivolous issues such as this.
Another trend which became apparent during the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) was that he was prepared to bring this government down on the basis of the restrained and moderate action it has taken as far as the labour situation is concerned. We have endeavoured, not only in the course of this trusteeship legislation but throughout the longshoremen's strike, to work out a voluntary rather than an imposed solution. This, to my way of thinking, is the antithesis of bureaucratic, arrogant action. Yet, apparently, the right hon. gentleman would prefer to bring down this government because it did not impose a public trusteeship by bureaucratic action months ago, before giving the individuals and the authorities concerned an opportunity to work the matter out. He considered, apparently, that the government should have moved in immediately. Had they done so, we can almost hear the screams of protest about bureaucracy. This situation makes it clear, in my opinion, how ridiculous is a motion such as we now find before us. It is not difficult in these circumstances to understand the lack of enthusiasm on the part of the right hon. gentleman's followers today. We all recognize what a fearful waste of time this lack of confidence motion really is. Indeed, it makes a mockery of the procedures of this house.
Today we heard the leader of the New Democratic party speak out in support of the action which has been taken by the government. The members of the N.D.P. hold themselves out as being the friends of labour, and

Labour Relations
they say they support the measured and restrained action this government has taken. I should like to read, from an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail less than a week ago. It is from an editorial which appeared in the issue of October 16 under the heading "Strong Performance":
When negotiation for a private trusteeship of Canadian maritime transport unions broke down last week, labour minister Allan J. MacEachen and the Canadian Labour Congress were subjected to outspoken and unreasonable criticism by United States labor secretary Willard Wirtz and Mr. George Meany, president of the American Federation of Labour-Congress of Industrial Organizations.
Legislation to establish government trusteeship aver the unions moved irrevocably through the House of Commons despite the U.S. criticism.
A strike by the international longshoremen's association crippled four St. Lawrence river ports and threatened to wreck the Canada-Russia grain deal. A mediator appointed by Mr. MacEachen moved into the picture and settled a strike that could have led to compulsory arbitration or more drastic federal government action.
Let us see how clearly the next paragraph is at variance with what the Leader of the Opposition had to say:
Mr. MacEachen, a 41-year-old former professor of economics, held a steady course under the strongest pressure of his political career. The I.L.A. settlement promises three years of peace. The trusteeship legislation shows strength of purpose to clean up the tangled waterfront mess according to the letter and spirit of the report by Mr. Justice T. G. Norris, who defined the problem and suggested the solution.
Members of Prime Minister Lester Pearson's cabinet have not always performed well under political fire. In a portfolio that needs a man with the confidence of the labour movement and the strength to deal with labour fearlessly, Mr. MacEachen's record so far gives reason for optimism for the future.
There we have an editorial dealing with the government's record and calling attention to this aspect as one of the brightest places in that record. Against such a background it becomes nonsense for the Leader of the Opposition to waste the time of this house by bringing in a want of confidence motion of the kind now before us, when there is ample evidence, from what has appeared in the press, and from what has been said by the leader of the New Democratic party, that the action taken by the government on this issue was restrained, and all that could be expected. So the exercise we see today seems a futile one.
Another reflection which occurred to me while I listened to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition was this: here is a man who for years has set himself up as a champion of the rights of the individual. Yet he inferred at the time of the longshoremen's strike last week that he wanted the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to move in and

impose compulsory arbitration before giving the parties themselves an opportunity to reach an agreed solution. As it turned out- probably to the disappointment of the Leader of the Opposition-the strike was settled without there being bureaucratic governmental intervention of the kind which the right hon. gentleman is supposed to detest so much. This speech comes from the man who is the author of the bill of rights. It is strange that a man responsible for a bill guaranteeing the rights of individuals should advocate compulsory arbitration before the parties concerned could work out a solution. This type of thinking was in evidence not only with regard to the longshoremen's strike but also to this trusteeship legislation. He would have had a solution imposed months ago before the parties had had a chance to settle the problem on a private basis. Should this be the attitude of a man who champions the rights of individuals? The bill of rights talks about freedom of association. Well, we have only to consider the longshoremen's strike last week. Here was a legal strike. The men started months ago going through all the conciliation processes available to them, until the time came then they had the legal right to strike. Before they had been out for two days the Leader of the Opposition wanted this government to move in and impose compulsory arbitration.
On this basis, we see how contradictory and frivolous was the speech made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition. I suggest the attitude of his followers amply indicates that there is no sincerity behind this particular want of confidence motion and I hope it will be disposed of as quickly as possible.

Mr. Speaker, we seem to be in a position where we are being lectured for bringing in an amendment to a supply motion. I understood that it was the leader of the house who proclaimed what the business would be. I thought it was he who laid down that there would be a supply motion every week, from now on, until they were all through.
We in the opposition are merely taking advantage of an opportunity which is rightfully ours. In doing so we have chosen to discuss a situation which is of the utmost importance to the economy of Canada today. We are taking advantage of this occasion to show the people of Canada why this particular situation has arisen, and who are responsible for this meaningless bungling or mishandling of the shipping problem on the great lakes. This is our rightful duty. It is our purpose. The hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) can call it a frivolous

issue if he likes. The Prime Minister can sit in his place and laugh about the problem facing Canada today, if he feels it is a laughing matter. The hon. member from Hamilton can call any issue affecting the economy of the country from coast to coast a frivolous issue, if he pleases. That may be his duty here; I do not know. However, I feel that as a representative of western Canada and of all Canada I should point out that corrective measures were not taken when they should have been taken to ensure the movement of exports from this country.
I should like to point out to the house that the great lakes shipping season will soon be drawing to a close. Is this bill going to be proclaimed at Christmas time when the issue is no longer of paramount importance owing to the freeze-up of the great lakes? We go along with the leader of the New Democratic party who commends the constructive purposes of the legislation. But why was the legislation necessary in the first place? We were told at the end of July that the legislation was ready to be brought in. But two months went by. Personally, I thought that two months would be all right, that perhaps it needed two months to get the various unions together and to a point where they could agree that the problem should be solved. But because of continued interference from across the line we got nowhere. I do not say that maliciously. We in western Canada are very fond of our neighbours to the south, but it is obvious that in recent months United States-Canadian relationships have not been too friendly. One has to look only at the headline of the Financial Post of October 19, 1963, to see the heading; "White House now thinks Canada is just a nuisance". Perhaps the Prime Minister called the President two or three times too often. Why should he have to call him at all? We are dealing with a Canadian matter of concern to our economy and exports. Some people laugh and call it a frivolous issue. Our wheat exports are tied up owing to meaningless bungling on the part of this government.
This whole issue should have been solved. It is all very well for the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) to tell us to pick up the Norris report and look at table 31 for the evidence. The evidence is certainly there. The report was tabled not too long ago; we now want action. Why has not the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) laid some charges on the evidence adduced before the Norris commission? He has been asked several times about this, and prompted and prodded by questions in the house, but no action has been forthcoming. The government waited till the 28902-5-245J

eleventh hour, until the dispute was irreconcilable. There is a headline in today's Globe and Mail which says:	"S.I.U. ordered by
Ottawa to halt the walk out at once". Anyone with any experience in handling men or experience in public relations or diplomacy would admit that handling people is perhaps the finest test of diplomacy. We know what a great diplomat the Prime Minister is held out to be, but the government brings in legislation which orders the S.I.U. to do things. You cannot order a group of men, Mr. Speaker, to do something and expect to receive their co-operation. You cannot order a group of men to go back to work.
The government had two months, from August to October, to get these groups together. But what did they do? They listened to Mr. Meany and Mr. Wirtz of the United States. They contacted the President several times. They dealt with Mr. Jodoin. But at no time are we told that they made actual efforts to get the five unions concerned together so that agreement could be reached. I do not know much about labour unions or labour matters-

It is always nice to know that someone is listening to you, Mr. Speaker-but I can say that two years ago the non-ops on the railroads were threatening to strike, and the government of that day brought in legislation, but before doing so made sure the union heads would agree to abide by it.
What are we told about the legislation recently passed? We are now waiting for it to be proclaimed. But according to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) the worst is yet to come. Not too long ago in the house he made that statement. This should all have been taken care of before now. The farmers of western Canada do not think this is a frivolous matter when their livelihood is at stake and the export of their prime product is held up. According to a late issue of the Union Farmer, a paper put out by the farmers' union of Saskatchewan, a call is made for more judicial settlement of this strike. That is a surprising thing to see in a Saskatchewan farmers' union paper, but the people are fed up and want the matter resolved. But it should not be handled in the meaningless bungling way of ordering people to go back to work. That is the worst thing which could be done with the S.I.U. men in their present frame of mind.
We have heard a lot of talk about voluntary trusteeship and the consultations had with Mr. Jodoin. Surprisingly enough we have not heard about the five other labour

Veterans Affairs
unions being consulted. Mr. Jodoin said the other day that a voluntary trusteeship is impossible now. The Prime Minister comes into the house today and tells us it is impossible; he accepts Mr. Jodoin's statement. Whether it is correct or not I do not know, but I do feel that there has been a great deal of meaningless bungling with regard to the handling of this whole issue. May I call it ten o'clock?
